title: Regime change as collective trader behavior shift
claim: Regime change is a significant change in collective trading behavior in financial markets, reflected in observable price dynamics and their statistical properties.
support: Stated as foundational premise; supported by observation that individual trader behavior is unobservable but collective behavior manifests in price statistics.
mechanism: Traders adjust positions or strategies in response to economic events or policy changes; collective effect shifts mean, volatility, and correlation of price movements.
assumptions: Price dynamics directly reflect collective trader behavior
Statistical properties of price movements can be used as proxies for regime identity
failure_modes: Regime definitions may be artifacts of chosen statistical framework
Multiple regimes may exist simultaneously in different market segments
validation: Authors demonstrate regime detection across multiple currencies and equity indices

title: Directional Change as event-driven alternative to fixed-interval time series
claim: Directional Change (DC) is a data-driven approach that samples prices at event-driven thresholds (price movements exceeding a threshold) rather than fixed time intervals, allowing tick-by-tick monitoring.
support: Formalized in Appendix A; contrasted with time series sampling; shown to extract information not visible in fixed-interval analysis.
mechanism: When price change magnitude exceeds threshold θ, a directional change event is recorded; events define intrinsic-time sampling points rather than wall-clock time.
assumptions: Threshold θ is stable or knowable a priori
DC events are meaningful economic markers (not noise)
Intrinsic-time scale is relevant to trading decisions
failure_modes: Threshold selection arbitrary and sensitive to market conditions
Very low thresholds may capture noise; high thresholds miss slow regime shifts
Does not adapt to regime-dependent volatility
validation: Authors demonstrate DC event detection on high-frequency FX data; compare with time-series sampling in empirical studies.

title: DC indicator R combines price movement and time duration
claim: The Directional Change indicator R measures return for each price trend, combining Total Price Movement (TMV) and Time to completion (T); both are orthogonal measures of volatility under DC.
support: Indicator R chosen by trial-and-error during methodology development; used as input to HMM for regime detection.
mechanism: R = f(TMV, T) where TMV is total magnitude and T is duration; log-transformed as LR[t] = log(R[t]) for HMM input.
assumptions: R is stationary or sufficiently stable for HMM fitting
Log transformation normalizes R distribution adequately
Combination of magnitude and duration is appropriate for regime identification
failure_modes: Trial-and-error selection not validated across other datasets
No sensitivity analysis on R functional form
Unknown how R behaves in regime-dependent volatility environments
validation: R tested on EUR-GBP, GBP-USD, EUR-USD 2016 data; successfully detects regime transitions missed by time-series volatility.

title: Realised volatility for time-series regime detection
claim: Realised Volatility (RV) computed from intra-day squared returns (e.g., 5-minute returns) serves as a time-series baseline for regime detection: RV(t) = sqrt(sum of squared intra-day returns).
support: Standard time-series volatility measure; used as comparison baseline to DC indicator in empirical study.
mechanism: Daily RV calculated as sqrt(sum of 5-minute squared log returns); fed into HMM alongside DC indicator for comparative regime detection.
assumptions: Intra-day returns capture regime volatility
Daily aggregation is appropriate time scale
Gaussian distribution assumption in HMM fits RV values
failure_modes: Daily aggregation loses intra-day regime transitions
RV may be biased by market microstructure noise
5-minute interval arbitrary; sensitive to choice
validation: Comparison study: RV regimes aligned with Brexit 2016 volatility spike but missed some transitions detected by DC.

title: Two-state HMM for regime inference from indicators
claim: A two-state Hidden Markov Model with Gaussian observation density is used to infer hidden regime states from DC indicator R or time-series volatility; HMM parameter fitting via EM algorithm using depmixS4 R package.
support: Method implemented on second-by-second FX data May-July 2016; regimes detected successfully during Brexit period.
mechanism: HMM assumes two hidden regimes (Regime 1, Regime 2) generate observations; Viterbi or posterior inference assigns state to each observation; transitions between states mark regime changes.
assumptions: Two regimes are sufficient for the observation period
Gaussian emission distribution fits indicator values
Markovian assumption (future depends only on current state) holds
EM convergence guarantees global optimum (not always true)
failure_modes: Two-state model may miss additional regimes
Model fitting may converge to local optima
Gaussian assumption may not hold for heavy-tailed distributions
No automatic selection of number of states; requires domain knowledge
validation: Successfully applied to EUR-GBP, GBP-USD, EUR-USD; detected 2016 Brexit-related regime changes; regimes align with market events.

title: Brexit 2016: DC and time-series regime detection comparison on FX data
claim: During the 2016 Brexit period (May-July 2016), DC-based regime detection identified the same major regime changes as time-series volatility but also detected additional regime transitions not visible in daily realized volatility; DC approach is at least as effective and often complementary.
support: Second-by-second data for EUR-GBP, GBP-USD, EUR-USD from CCFEA/Kibot; both approaches detected volatility spike on June 24, 2016 (referendum result); DC detected additional finer-grained transitions.
mechanism: UK referendum June 23 resulted in unexpected exit vote; GBP plunged 30-year low; global stock sell-offs triggered. Both DC and RV indicators spiked during this period, indicating Regime 2 (higher volatility).
assumptions: Regime change definition (statistical shift) captures economically significant events
Two-state model sufficient for 2-month window
Threshold θ=0.4% appropriate for FX markets
failure_modes: Regimes may not be economically interpretable
Regime timing and boundaries depend on indicator and model choices
No causal link between identified regimes and trading performance established
validation: Study period well-documented historical event; regimes align with market news; replicable with public FX data and standard HMM tools.

title: Normal vs. Abnormal regime classification potential
claim: Regimes detected via DC+HMM can be classified into Normal (lower volatility, stable pricing) and Abnormal (crisis, high volatility) categories; this classification may identify early warning signals for market stress.
support: Authors characterize market regimes on 10 different markets; show statistical separation in indicator space between low- and high-volatility regimes.
mechanism: Regime 1 exhibits lower DC return R and lower realized volatility; Regime 2 exhibits higher values. Indicator-space clustering reveals distinct regime phenotypes.
assumptions: Two regimes map cleanly to normal/abnormal dichotomy
Volatility is a reliable proxy for market stress
Classification generalizes across markets and time periods
failure_modes: Regime 1 may contain multiple sub-regimes
Normal/abnormal boundary is continuous, not discrete
Regimes may shift meaning depending on asset class, time period, or market microstructure
validation: Multi-market regime characterization (Ch4) shows consistent separation; but validation against known crisis periods incomplete in book.

title: Multi-market regime analysis: normal vs. abnormal phenotypes
claim: Analysis across 10 financial markets shows that Regime 1 (lower volatility) and Regime 2 (higher volatility) exhibit consistent statistical phenotypes (indicator ranges, distributions) when parameters like DC threshold θ are held constant.
support: Authors tested on multiple equity indices, FX pairs, and time periods; regime properties consistent; suggests transferability.
mechanism: Regimes defined by statistical distribution of indicator R under different market conditions; high-volatility regime has higher mean and variance of R.
assumptions: Threshold θ=0.4% is universal or near-universal
Two regimes suffice across all tested markets
Indicator R is invariant to asset class and time period
failure_modes: Regime parameters may be market- or time-dependent
Parameter transfer to new markets/assets risky without validation
Seasonality, microstructure changes not analyzed
validation: Tested on DJIA, FTSE 100, S&P 500, EUR-GBP, GBP-USD, EUR-USD, etc.; consistency observed but may not hold in novel asset classes (crypto, commodities) or post-2020 markets.

title: Real-time regime tracking for market monitoring
claim: Directional Change indicators combined with a Naive Bayes classifier enable real-time, tick-by-tick regime tracking; probability thresholds (e.g., B-Simple, B-Strict variants) allow tunable sensitivity for early-warning signals.
support: Authors implement two variants of Naive Bayes classifier; test on DJIA, FTSE 100, S&P 500; successfully track regime transitions in real time.
mechanism: For each DC trend, compute probability of being in each regime via Naive Bayes; threshold probability to generate regime label; variants B-Simple and B-Strict trade off false positives vs. false negatives.
assumptions: Naive Bayes independence assumption holds for regime features
Historical frequency statistics are predictive of future regime membership
Probability thresholds can be tuned to desired sensitivity
failure_modes: Independence assumption violated if regime features are correlated
Past regime statistics may not predict future (non-stationary)
Lag between indicator and actual regime change not quantified
High false-positive rate may trigger spurious trading signals
validation: Tested on equity indices; regime transitions tracked successfully; but latency and false-positive rate for live systems not thoroughly analyzed.

title: Regime tracking lag and classification variants
claim: When regime transitions are tracked via Naive Bayes probability thresholds, there is inherent lag between regime onset and detection; B-Simple (immediate classification) and B-Strict (conservative thresholds) variants exhibit different lag-accuracy trade-offs.
support: Empirical testing on DJIA, FTSE 100, S&P 500 shows B-Simple has faster detection but higher false-positives; B-Strict is more conservative.
mechanism: B-Simple uses looser probability thresholds for immediate classification; B-Strict requires higher confidence; both inherit lag from Naive Bayes inference on accumulated DC trends.
assumptions: Lag is tolerable for intended trading system (minutes to hours)
Threshold tuning can be automated or learned from historical data
failure_modes: B-Simple may trigger too many false regime alarms
B-Strict may miss early-warning opportunities
Lag may expand during low-volume periods or regime transitions
No principled way to select threshold without labeled regime data
validation: Comparative backtest results shown for indices; but optimal threshold not determined; post-implementation tuning recommended.

title: Regime change signals can reduce drawdown in algorithmic trading
claim: Algorithmic trading strategies that incorporate regime change signals (specifically, regime transitions detected via DC+Naive Bayes) can reduce maximum drawdown and improve risk-adjusted returns compared to control strategies that ignore regime changes.
support: Authors backtest two regime-aware trading algorithms (JC1, JC2) against control algorithm (CT1) on equity data; regime-aware variants exhibit lower maximum drawdown.
mechanism: Regime-aware algorithms enter/exit positions on regime transitions; when regime shifts to abnormal (high volatility), algorithm may reduce exposure or tighten stops; this lowers peak losses.
assumptions: Regime transitions are predictive of future price movements or volatility
Entry/exit rules based on regime changes are optimal or near-optimal
Backtest assumptions (no slippage, instant fills, fixed transaction costs) hold in live trading
Money management (fixed lot size) is appropriate
failure_modes: Regime-aware rules may not outperform in regimes with trending opportunities
Backtest overfitting: rules tuned to specific dataset
Transition lag may cause late entries/exits, reducing effectiveness
Transaction costs and slippage not modeled; may erase gains
No statistical significance test of performance differences
validation: Book demonstrates drawdown reduction in backtests; but claims proof-of-concept only. Real-world validation with transaction costs, slippage, and regime shift non-stationarity needed.

title: Trading algorithms JC1 and JC2 regime-entry/exit rules
claim: Two trading algorithms are proposed: JC1 enters/exits trades immediately upon regime transition detection; JC2 employs a lagged entry/exit to reduce false positives. Both use fixed lot sizing and hold positions until next regime change.
support: Algorithms tested on equity indices; detailed in methods section; comparison backtests provided.
mechanism: JC1: Entry signal on regime transition to Regime 1 (normal); exit on transition to Regime 2 (abnormal). JC2: Same but with delay to reduce whipsaws.
assumptions: Regime transitions are tradeable entry/exit signals
Regime 1 corresponds to profitable trading periods; Regime 2 to loss periods
Fixed lot size is sufficient risk management
Costs (bid-ask, commissions) are negligible or constant
failure_modes: Algorithms may be overfit to backtest period
Regime definitions may not hold in live trading
Entry/exit delays may reduce profitability
Fixed sizing does not adapt to volatility or regime-dependent risk
validation: Backtested; but authors acknowledge proof-of-concept status. No live trading results or post-sample validation provided.

title: Proof-of-concept trading algorithms lack realistic market assumptions
claim: The trading algorithms presented (JC1, JC2) are proof-of-concept demonstrations; they do not account for transaction costs, slippage, partial fills, market impact, or other real-world execution friction that typically erode profitability.
support: Experimental setup specifies fixed money management and simple entry/exit rules; no slippage model or commission structure described.
mechanism: Realistic execution incurs bid-ask spread, commissions, market impact on large orders, and partial fills. These costs can flip backtested gains into losses.
assumptions: Backtest conditions approximate real-world execution
failure_modes: Algorithms likely to underperform in live trading
Study overstates profitability and edge
Risk management (drawdown control) may not hold under realistic costs
validation: Standard practice in backtesting: results are optimistic without slippage/costs. Independent validation with realistic market model needed before live deployment.

title: DC threshold selection is critical but not systematized
claim: The Directional Change threshold θ significantly affects regime detection results; in studies, θ is chosen arbitrarily (e.g., 0.4%) but no principled methodology for threshold selection across markets or time periods is provided.
support: Authors note θ=0.4% chosen arbitrarily; reference prior work (Glattfelder et al.) suggests power law in DC observations implies same stylized facts at different thresholds.
mechanism: Low θ captures noise; high θ misses slow drifts. Optimal θ depends on volatility regime, asset class, and trading time scale.
assumptions: θ is stable or knowable a priori for new markets
Power law suggests similar patterns across thresholds
failure_modes: Threshold transfer to new markets without validation risky
No adaptive threshold mechanism for time-varying volatility
Parameter sensitivity analysis missing
validation: Authors suggest power law implies threshold robustness but do not empirically validate. Sensitivity analysis on θ across datasets needed.

title: DC and time-series approaches are complementary for market monitoring
claim: Directional Change and time-series analysis detect regime changes via different statistical lenses; DC detects transitions missed by time series and vice versa; using both approaches together provides richer market intelligence.
support: Empirical evidence from Brexit study (Ch3) shows DC identified regimes not detected by daily realized volatility; authors recommend dual-method approach.
mechanism: DC samples at event-driven times (intrinsic time); time series samples at fixed intervals (wall-clock time). Different sampling rates reveal different regime transitions.
assumptions: Both methods capture economically meaningful signals
Complementarity is consistent across markets and periods
failure_modes: Dual approach increases complexity and potential for false signals
Complementarity may not generalize beyond Brexit period
Reconciling conflicting signals from two methods requires domain judgment
validation: Demonstrated on FX data 2016; generalization to other asset classes, time periods, and market conditions untested.

title: Early-warning system potential for financial stability
claim: Combining DC-based regime tracking with Naive Bayes classification could form the basis of an early-warning system for regulators and market participants to detect shifts toward abnormal market regimes and take precautionary actions.
support: Authors identify early-warning system as future research direction; mention potential for regulators to react to regime transitions.
mechanism: Real-time tick-by-tick regime tracking generates regime-transition alerts; alerts can trigger monitoring escalation, hedging, or circuit-breaker activation.
assumptions: Regime transitions are predictive of market stress or crashes
Early warning is actionable (provides time to respond)
False-positive rate is acceptable for operational use
failure_modes: System may trigger too frequently, causing alert fatigue
Lag in detection may reduce usefulness
Regimes may not be causal predictors of market moves
Regulatory implementation requires infrastructure and coordination
validation: Concept discussed but not tested; validation against real financial crises and regulatory deployment scenarios needed.
